title: Closure of ocean–crust fluid and biogeochemical exchange

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a globally constrained account of how seawater enters the oceanic crust, circulates through its connected pore spaces and fractures, reacts with rock, sediments and microorganisms, and returns to the ocean. Closing this account means measuring fluid and heat transport together with net chemical changes, then showing how the resulting exchanges fit into ocean-wide budgets with explicit uncertainties. The central scope is the basaltic ridge-flank aquifer, including recharge, transport, discharge and exchange with overlying sediments.

The crust acts as a continuous-flow chemical and biological reactor: flowing seawater supplies reactants and removes reaction products, while conditions along its path influence both water–rock reactions and microbial activity. The desired capability would connect these processes quantitatively, distinguishing their contributions to net exchange rather than inferring a global budget from fluid circulation alone. It would require representative coverage across crustal ages, temperatures and flow regimes; a well-characterized individual borehole or discharge site cannot establish global closure.

significance.text: The potential importance comes from the enormous amount of water processed, even where its composition changes only slightly. Fisher and Wheat's 2010 review estimated ridge-flank discharge at roughly 10^16 kilograms per year, compared with approximately 4 × 10^16 kilograms per year of global river discharge. These are comparable orders of magnitude, not equal flows. Moreover, crustal circulation largely recycles seawater; the comparison does not make it an equivalent freshwater input. Its chemical significance depends on the element and the reactions encountered along the flow path.

The system also supports a substantial subsurface biosphere. Robador's November 2024 review reports earlier estimates of approximately 1.6 gigatonnes of carbon in living prokaryotic biomass and a crustal biosphere volume nearly 2% of ocean volume. These estimates describe the broader crustal biosphere, not a separately measured ridge-flank biomass inventory, and the underlying primary determinations were not included in the supplied evidence. They indicate potential scale, but biomass and habitable volume alone do not establish metabolic rates or net chemical fluxes. Describing this reservoir as a hidden ocean is therefore a metaphor, not a measured equivalence to the ocean's water inventory or productivity.

If representative global closure were achieved, it would turn a poorly constrained ocean boundary into an observationally constrained exchange term for magnesium, alkalinity, carbon, iron and other elements. Separating water–rock, sedimentary and microbial contributions could substantially revise particular element budgets and establish whether microbial processing is a minor contribution or a major pathway under specified conditions. Ocean biogeochemical models could incorporate those exchanges with explicit uncertainty instead of relying on poorly resolved global extrapolations.

Conditional synthesis: better crustal exchange constraints could improve interpretations of ocean carbon cycling and long-term ocean chemistry, but their downstream value would depend on the accuracy of other model components and on how exchange changes over time. Closure for selected elements would not establish large crustal fluxes for every element, guarantee predictive accuracy under future conditions, or independently predict climate. The revolutionary advance would be the measured planetary budget and process attribution; its comparative ranking against other oceanographic breakthroughs remains qualitative.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is representative global measurement and integration of fluid transport, reactions and microbial rates. High-temperature axial springs account for only a small fraction of the seafloor hydrothermal advective heat output estimated in the 2010 review. Ridge-flank circulation transports much larger, generally cooler fluid fluxes, but has sparse direct measurements. It should not be pictured as uniformly diffuse leakage: much thermally important exchange is focused through exposed basement outcrops, although diffuse seepage also occurs.

A global account must resolve how recharge and discharge sites connect through the crust and how much water travels along different pathways. Chemical effects vary with temperature, residence time, sediment interaction and the element being tracked. Consequently, a heat or water-flow estimate cannot by itself determine net solute exchange. Narrowly sampled pairs of recharge and discharge features can give an overly idealized picture of the aquifer, leaving the representativeness of regional and global extrapolations uncertain.

Uncontaminated access to fluids in old ocean crust remains a major challenge in the November 2024 review. Microbial observations also need to connect biological potential with activity: genomic evidence can identify possible metabolisms, while rate measurements are needed to quantify actual processing under relevant conditions. Local metabolic measurements already exist, but sparse access and sampling limit their conversion into representative global rates.

The attribution problem is coupled to the transport problem. Microorganisms, basalt reactions and sediment exchange can affect the same chemical species, and fluid flow controls reactant replenishment and product removal. A convincing account must reconcile these processes with the observed net chemical change without counting linked transformations as independent contributions. Measuring biomass, detecting metabolic genes or identifying a reaction pathway is insufficient to assign its share of the exported flux.

current_state.text: Fisher and Wheat's 2010 review estimated low-temperature ridge-flank fluid discharge at about three orders of magnitude greater than high-temperature axial discharge. This is a comparison of estimated fluid discharge, not a claim that heat transport or every chemical flux differs by the same factor. The review also documented few direct measurements of fluid fluxes and chemical compositions from typical ridge-flank systems and emphasized that detailed work at two discussed sites concentrated on individual pairs of features. Those findings establish the historical scale and sampling problem, not a verified count of accessible sites in 2026.

Robador's review, published on 27 November 2024, documents achieved access through CORK borehole observatories, drilled cores and exposed outcrop seeps. CORK installations and arrays provide repeated access for sampling and experiments. Genomic studies and local activity measurements have advanced understanding of the crustal biosphere, so the unresolved capability is not the first observation of microbial metabolism. It is representative quantitative attribution of that activity to global biogeochemical exchange, which the review describes as still largely speculative.

The supplied evidence establishes substantial observational capabilities and an outstanding global quantification gap through November 2024. It does not establish that the proposed closure had been achieved, nor does it establish its exact status on 1 November 2026. The supplied review assessed complete retained text for the 2010 and 2024 papers; its 2010 conclusions relied on prose rather than uninspected graphics. Retrieval of those older papers in 2026 does not itself update their scientific conclusions.

The research notes additionally cite a chapter dated 4 November 2025 and describe a publisher summary as reiterating large flank-to-axial fluid-flux differences and unresolved architectural and chemical parameters. No retained chapter text or publisher-summary artifact accompanies that citation, and the supplied review could not inspect its identity or contents. It therefore cannot substantiate a new 2025 result or extend the verified current-state account. This access limitation is not evidence that the chapter's reported claims are false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: quantify recharge, discharge, heat transport and net major chemical exchange across representative young and old crust, temperatures and flow regimes, including exchange with overlying sediments. Regional studies should establish internally consistent transport-and-reaction budgets before being combined into global estimates. The coverage and upscaling should be sufficient to test whether well-studied sites represent the wider aquifer. Agreement at a few drilled sites would demonstrate local capability, not global closure.
completion_criteria.label: Representative regional transport-and-reaction budgets support global aquifer exchange estimates

completion_criteria.text: Proposed budget test: integrate the resulting exchanges into global magnesium, alkalinity and carbon budgets over an explicitly defined interval. Include river inputs, sedimentary exchange, other material sources and sinks, and changes in ocean inventories during that interval. Fluxes must be integrated over time or compared with inventory-change rates; a flux cannot be compared directly with an inventory uncertainty because their units differ. Require residuals to fall within a prespecified propagated uncertainty small enough to distinguish competing estimates of crustal exchange. The choice of elements and tolerance is a proposal, not an established acceptance standard.
completion_criteria.label: Global magnesium, alkalinity and carbon budgets close within prespecified uncertainty

completion_criteria.text: Proposed microbial attribution test: pair direct metabolic-rate measurements with fluid transport and chemical reaction constraints across representative environments. Estimate how much of the measured net exchange involves microbial processing, while accounting for coupled abiotic reactions and sediment transformations. Genomic potential and biomass estimates should provide context rather than substitute for measured rates. Attribution should specify what is being counted so that a sequence of coupled processes is not counted repeatedly as separate net fluxes.
completion_criteria.label: Measured metabolic rates quantify microbial contributions to net exchange

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: make sampling methods, contamination controls, rate calculations, transport assumptions and uncertainty propagation available for independent assessment. Seek agreement among repeated observations, independent methods and predictions tested at sites outside the initial calibration set. Report which ages, environments, elements and time intervals the demonstration covers, together with remaining gaps and sensitivity to unsampled regimes. Finite observations can establish demonstrated breadth and defensible global extrapolation; they cannot establish literal universality or guarantee future behavior.
completion_criteria.label: Make methods assessable and report reproducibility evidence and extrapolation limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: OCE-01, A closed theory of oceanic turbulent transport, concerns transport within ocean water, whereas OCE-05 concerns exchange through the crustal boundary and reactions along subsurface pathways. Both need transport constraints, but a successful turbulent-transport theory would not by itself determine crustal permeability, fluid chemistry or microbial rates. OCE-02, Synoptic sensing of the ocean interior, could supply ocean-side context for discharge and its dispersal; broad interior observations would still need dedicated subsurface access to close the aquifer budget.

Roster-based synthesis: OCE-03, A predictive closure of the biological carbon pump, overlaps through ocean carbon accounting, while OCE-05 addresses carbon transformations and exchanges involving the crustal aquifer. OCE-09, A predictive theory of pelagic size structure and trophic transfer, addresses water-column ecological organization. Neither pelagic trophic predictions nor biological-pump closure substitutes for measuring microbial processing in basaltic crust, although their carbon budgets could eventually be coupled.

Roster-based synthesis: OCE-04, Persistent mobile operations at full ocean depth, could enable repeated visits to deep seafloor access points. OCE-10, Basin-scale underwater positioning without surfacing, could support sustained navigation and repeat surveys, while OCE-08, Continuous centimeter-level geodesy of the seismogenic seafloor, concerns precise seafloor deformation measurements. These are distinct operational or measurement capabilities; none alone establishes fluid-and-reaction closure. The supplied roster identifies OCE-04 as an operations concept, and the supplied evidence does not verify the research notes' separate attribution of a 2025 hadal-seep result to it.

Roster-based synthesis: OCE-06, A verified law of ice-shelf basal melting, addresses heat-driven exchange at an ice–ocean boundary. OCE-07, The stability class of the global overturning circulation, concerns the behavior of large-scale ocean circulation. They share the need for well-constrained transport and boundary processes, but their governing questions differ from quantifying crustal circulation and chemical reactions. Completing OCE-05 would not establish either a basal-melting law or an overturning stability class.

Scope synthesis: coastal submarine groundwater discharge from land aquifers and sediment-hosted hadal seep systems are excluded from the proposed basaltic ridge-flank closure, while sediment–basement exchange along ridge-flank flow paths remains included. These exclusions define the intended accounting boundary. The supplied evidence does not establish the historical disposition of coastal groundwater research or the particular 2025 hadal result mentioned in the notes.

change_log.change: Preserved OCE-05's identity and expanded closure into a coupled recharge, transport, discharge, sediment-exchange and reaction budget.
change_log.reason: The research and review support a global observational capability whose scope exceeds measurements at individual discharge sites.

change_log.change: Qualified the description of ridge-flank flow as diffuse and specified the denominator for the axial heat comparison.
change_log.reason: Thermally important exchange commonly focuses through exposed basement outcrops, and the small axial fraction refers to estimated seafloor hydrothermal advective heat output.

change_log.change: Retained the three-orders-of-magnitude discharge comparison as a dated 2010 estimate and added the supported river-flow quantities.
change_log.reason: Fluid discharge, heat transport and chemical flux are different quantities; comparable water throughput does not imply equal freshwater input or equal chemical effects.

change_log.change: Attributed the 1.6 Gt C and nearly 2% volume estimates to the broader crustal biosphere and identified their review-reported provenance.
change_log.reason: They are not separately measured ridge-flank inventories, and the underlying primary studies were not supplied.

change_log.change: Distinguished demonstrated access, genomic studies and local metabolic measurements from unresolved global microbial attribution.
change_log.reason: The evidence documents existing biological measurements; the gap concerns representativeness, rates and contributions to net global exchange.

change_log.change: Bound the supported current-state account to November 2024 and retained the 2025 chapter only as an explicitly uninspected citation.
change_log.reason: The supplied record contains no inspectable 2025 chapter or summary and no freshness evidence establishing November 2026 status.

change_log.change: Replaced comparison with seawater inventory uncertainty by a time-defined budget with inventory changes and propagated uncertainty.
change_log.reason: Flux and inventory have different units, and closure requires all material budget terms plus a meaningful uncertainty threshold.

change_log.change: Added explicit treatment of coupled microbial and abiotic processes, independent reproduction and limits of finite demonstrations.
change_log.reason: Process attribution can double count linked reactions, and local agreement or broad finite testing cannot establish universal closure.

change_log.change: Mapped relationships to every other supplied roster entry and corrected the treatment of OCE-04.
change_log.reason: The roster defines OCE-04 as full-depth mobile operations; no supplied evidence establishes its alleged 2025 hadal-seep result.

change_log.change: Preserved the proposed impact while qualifying model accuracy, climate implications and element-specific importance.
change_log.reason: A constrained crustal boundary could revise ocean budgets without guaranteeing comprehensive prediction or large fluxes for every element.

unresolved_issues: Whether representative global closure or major advances beyond the November 2024 evidence had been demonstrated by 1 November 2026 is not established by the supplied record.
The identity, contents and claimed publisher-summary statements of the cited 2025 chapter remain unverified because no retained artifact was supplied. Its assertions are not treated as disproven.
The primary determinations underlying the reported 1.6 Gt C biomass and nearly 2% biosphere-volume estimates were not supplied for independent assessment.
The representative sampling design, averaging interval, uncertainty tolerance and precision needed to distinguish competing global crustal-flux estimates remain to be specified.
An operational accounting convention for coupled microbial, sedimentary and water–rock contributions is still needed to avoid double counting.
The supplied material does not verify coastal groundwater's historical disposition or the alleged 2025 hadal-seep result associated in the notes with OCE-04.

The review recommended removing the uninspectable 2025 summary. Its scientific assertions were excluded from the established account, but the citation and access limitation were retained to preserve provenance and uncertainty.
No historical calibration examples were supplied for ranking this innovation's revolutionary significance against other breakthroughs; that comparison remains qualitative.

brief.title: Accounting for the ocean’s exchange with buried rock
possible: Scientists could trace how seawater travels through rock beneath the seabed and measure what changes before it returns. They could build a worldwide account of the water, heat and chemicals exchanged, including the effects of microbes and the sediment covering the rock.
why: Huge amounts of seawater circulate beneath the seabed. Even small chemical changes along the way can matter for ocean chemistry. Measuring this exchange would give ocean scientists a firmer account of where carbon and other elements go.
Scientists could also establish how much underground microbes contribute to those changes. Ocean models could then include measured exchanges and their uncertainty.

sources.who: Andrew T. Fisher and C. Geoffrey Wheat
sources.showed: Their review describes how exposed volcanic rock channels seawater through the crust away from spreading ridges, where new seafloor forms. Field studies connect water flow, temperature and chemical change.
sources.quote:
Seamounts and other basement outcrops focus ridge-flank 
hydrothermal exchange between the crust and the ocean.
sources.cited_for: It supports the scale of circulation and the importance of exposed rock as a route between the ocean and buried crust.
sources.not_established: Local studies do not establish a representative worldwide account of water transport and chemical exchange.

sources.showed: His review brings together observations of active microbes beneath the seabed and describes access through drilled observatories, rock samples and natural seeps.
sources.quote: Underlying the thick sediment layer in ocean basins, the flow of seawater through the cracked and porous upper igneous crust supports a previously hidden and largely unexplored active subsurface microbial biome.
sources.cited_for: It supports the presence of active microbial communities and the ability to sample and study them.
sources.not_established: The share of worldwide chemical exchange caused by microbial activity remains largely speculative.

sources.showed: A later version of the same work.
This chapter concerns differences in water flow between spreading ridges and their flanks, alongside unresolved flow pathways and chemical changes.
sources.cited_for: It concerns the scale of circulation and unresolved controls on exchange.
sources.not_established: Large water flows alone do not establish how much chemical exchange occurs.

shown: Fisher and Wheat connected local measurements of water flow, heat and chemistry at studied sites. Robador describes repeated sampling and experiments through drilled observatories, alongside studies of microbial activity. Scientists can investigate individual systems, but a representative worldwide account remains unresolved.
missing: Measurements must cover the range of crust ages, temperatures and flow pathways well enough to support worldwide estimates.
Water and heat measurements still need to be joined with net chemical changes, including exchange with overlying sediment.
Measured microbial activity must be linked to chemical exchange without counting connected reactions more than once.

milestones.label: Regional measurements support worldwide estimates
milestones.explanation: Representative regions would have to yield consistent accounts of water, heat and chemical exchange across different crust ages and conditions. This would establish whether local findings can support worldwide estimates.

milestones.label: Global chemical accounts balance within agreed uncertainty
milestones.explanation: Global accounts of magnesium, carbon and alkalinity, water’s capacity to neutralize acid, would have to balance within a preset uncertainty over a defined interval. This would test crustal exchange against other ocean gains and losses.

milestones.label: Measured microbial activity explains its share of exchange
milestones.explanation: Measurements of microbial reaction rates would have to explain their contribution alongside water flow, rock reactions and sediment effects. This would quantify the biological share without counting linked changes repeatedly.

milestones.label: Independent checks establish reliability and limits
milestones.explanation: Methods and uncertainty calculations would have to withstand independent assessment, with repeated observations and successful tests at additional sites. This would establish reproducibility and the limits of worldwide estimates.

uncertain: The sampling coverage, averaging interval and precision needed to distinguish competing worldwide estimates remain to be defined.
Scientists still need a shared way to assign chemical changes among microbes, rock and sediment when their reactions are linked.
